AVGO coverage: No direct company-specific mapping; use handbook guidance and add your own evidence.
Meaning: A description of  what  the company sells,  to whom ,  how  it delivers it, and  how it gets paid . If you can’t explain it in two sentences, you don’t understand it yet.
Interpretation: The business model determines margins, capital needs, cyclicality and how durable revenue is.
Cautions: Management’s description can be marketing. Check it against where the revenue and profit actually come from (segment data).

AVGO coverage: No direct company-specific mapping; use handbook guidance and add your own evidence.
Meaning: The mechanism by which the company earns revenue:  one-time sales ,  recurring subscriptions ,  usage-based  fees,  transaction  take-rates,  advertising ,  licensing ,  hardware + services .
Interpretation: Recurring and contractual revenue is more predictable and usually valued at higher multiples than one-off or project revenue.
Cautions: “Recurring” is sometimes stretched to cover repeat-but-uncontracted purchases.

Meaning: The distinct parts of the company that management reports separately (by product line or geography), each with its own revenue and usually operating profit.
Interpretation: Segments often have very different growth, margins and risk. A great segment can be hidden inside a mediocre consolidated number — or vice versa.
Cautions: Corporate costs are often not allocated to segments, so segment profits add up to more than total operating income.

AVGO coverage: No direct company-specific mapping; use handbook guidance and add your own evidence.
Meaning: How total revenue splits across products, segments, geographies, customer types, or recurring vs one-off.
Interpretation: A shift in mix toward higher-margin products raises overall margins even if nothing else changes (“mix shift”).
Cautions: Margin improvement from mix shift is not the same as improvement in each business.

AVGO coverage: No direct company-specific mapping; use handbook guidance and add your own evidence.
Handbook formula:
Revenue = Customers × Revenue per Customer
(or Units × Price)
Meaning: The specific levers that can grow revenue:  market expansion ,  price increases ,  customer growth ,  more spend per customer ,  new products ,  geographic expansion ,  acquisitions .
Interpretation: Good analysis names the  one or two drivers that matter most  and checks the evidence for each.
Cautions: Growth bought via acquisitions or driven by price alone can fade; organic volume growth is usually higher quality.

AVGO coverage: No direct company-specific mapping; use handbook guidance and add your own evidence.
Meaning: Anything that lets a company win customers or earn better economics than competitors: better product, lower cost, brand, distribution, technology.
Interpretation: A competitive advantage becomes a  moat  only when it is  durable  — hard for competitors to copy for many years.
Cautions: A temporary lead (a hot product) is not the same as a durable structural advantage.

Meaning: A  durable  structural advantage that protects a company’s profits and returns on capital from competition over many years — like a moat protecting a castle.
Interpretation: The financial evidence of a moat is  high ROIC sustained for many years , stable or rising margins, and pricing power.
Cautions: “No competition” is NOT automatically a moat.  The important question is:  WHY is competition difficult?  If high profits exist and nothing stops others from copying, competitors will come.
Related cards: roic, competition, market-share, business-model, competitive-advantage, ev-revenue
Additional guidance:
Source of moat  What it means  Typical examples
           Network Effects   Each new user makes the product more valuable for others.  Marketplaces, payment networks, social platforms
           Switching Costs   Leaving is painful, risky or expensive.  ERP software, core banking, embedded workflows
           Economies of Scale   Unit costs fall with size; small rivals can’t match prices profitably.  Warehouse retail, cloud infrastructure, chips
           Brand   Customers pay more or choose by default because of trust/status.  Luxury goods, beverages, consumer tech
           Intellectual Property   Patents, trade secrets, proprietary technology.  Pharma, semiconductor design
           Cost Advantage   Structurally lower costs from process, location or resources.  Low-cost producers, unique mines
           Distribution   Owns the channel or shelf; reaches customers cheaper.  Consumer staples, app stores
           Vertical Integration   Controls key parts of the value chain → cost, speed, quality.  EVs, aerospace, fashion
           Regulatory Barriers   Licenses or laws limit who can compete.  Utilities, exchanges, defence, rating agencies
           Data Advantage   Proprietary data improves the product and compounds with usage.  Search, credit scoring, mapping

AVGO coverage: No direct company-specific mapping; use handbook guidance and add your own evidence.
Handbook formula: Market Share = Company Revenue / Total Market Revenue
Meaning: The company’s portion of total sales in its market.
Interpretation: Rising share = winning against competitors. Leading share can bring scale advantages.
Cautions: Depends heavily on how you define “the market”. Share can be bought with unprofitable price cuts.

AVGO coverage: No direct company-specific mapping; use handbook guidance and add your own evidence.
Meaning: The total annual revenue available for a product if the company captured the entire market. Related:  SAM  (serviceable) and  SOM  (realistically obtainable).
Interpretation: TAM sets the ceiling on long-term growth. A small company in a big, growing TAM has a long runway.
Cautions: Company-presented TAMs are often hugely inflated. Build your own bottom-up estimate.

AVGO coverage: No direct company-specific mapping; use handbook guidance and add your own evidence.
Meaning: The other companies (and substitutes) competing for the same customers, and how they compete: price, product, distribution, brand.
Interpretation: Intense competition pushes margins and returns down toward the cost of capital unless a moat protects the company.
Cautions: New entrants and substitutes from other industries are often missed.

Meaning: The share of revenue coming from the largest customers. Companies must disclose customers above 10% of revenue.
Interpretation: High concentration gives big customers bargaining power and creates a cliff risk if one leaves.
Cautions: Concentration can rise quietly as a big customer grows faster than others.

Meaning: The tendency of revenue and profits to rise and fall with the economy or an industry cycle (commodities, autos, semiconductors, housing, airlines).
Interpretation: For cyclicals, today’s earnings may be at a peak or trough — so valuation on current earnings can mislead.
Cautions: Cyclicals often look  cheapest (low P/E) at the peak  and most expensive at the bottom.

AVGO coverage: No direct company-specific mapping; use handbook guidance and add your own evidence.
Meaning: Specific, ideally dated, events that could change how the market sees the company: earnings, product launches, margin inflection, spin-offs, buybacks, regulatory decisions, index inclusion.
Interpretation: Without a catalyst, an undervalued stock can stay undervalued for a long time. That delay alone is not a value trap; investigate whether lasting economic damage undermines the valuation.
Cautions: Catalysts that everyone already knows about are usually priced in.

AVGO coverage: No direct company-specific mapping; use handbook guidance and add your own evidence.
Meaning: The main things that could hurt the business or the stock:  competition, technology disruption, regulation, debt, customer concentration, margin compression, dilution, cyclicality, execution risk .
Interpretation: The 10-K Risk Factors list is long and legalistic; your job is to pick the 3–5 that actually matter and how likely/severe they are.
Cautions: The risk that sinks a company is often not on the list — think about what could disrupt the model.
Related cards: invalidation, customer-concentration, debt, cyclicality, thesis-def, circle-of-competence, required-return

AVGO coverage: 12 calculated records; 10 reported records (includes unavailable rows)
Handbook formula: Revenue Growth = (Current Revenue − Previous Revenue) / Previous Revenue
Meaning: The total amount a company earns from selling its products or services during a period,  before any expenses  are subtracted. The first line of the income statement — the “top line”.
Interpretation: YoY (Year over Year)  compares a period with the same period a year earlier (Q2 2026 vs Q2 2025) — removes seasonality.  QoQ (Quarter over Quarter)  compares with the immediately preceding quarter (Q2 vs Q1) — shows momentum but is distorted by seasonality.
Cautions: Revenue ≠ Profit.  Growth can be inflated by acquisitions, currency moves, price-only increases, or one-off contracts. High growth with deep losses can destroy value.
Where to find: First line of the income statement.
Related cards: cogs, growth-drivers, tam, profitable-growth, backlog, revenue-recognition

Meaning: The  direct  costs associated with generating revenue — costs that rise and fall with each unit sold. “COGS” is used for physical goods; “Cost of Revenue” is the broader term that also covers services.
Interpretation: Revenue − Cost of Revenue = Gross Profit. The lower COGS is relative to revenue, the more each sale contributes to everything else.
Cautions: Companies classify costs differently (e.g. shipping, support), which makes peer comparisons tricky.

Handbook formula: Gross Profit = Revenue − Cost of Revenue
Meaning: What remains from revenue after paying the direct costs of producing the product or service. It is the pool of money that must pay for R&D, sales, administration, interest, taxes — and profit.
Interpretation: Gross profit should grow at least as fast as revenue. If it grows slower, direct costs are rising faster than prices.
Cautions: A big gross profit does not mean the company is profitable — operating expenses can consume all of it.
Where to find: Often shown directly; otherwise Revenue − Cost of Revenue.

Handbook formula: Operating Income = Gross Profit − Operating Expenses
Meaning: Costs of running and growing the business that are  not directly tied to each unit sold :  R&D  — Research & Development: engineers, new products, technology.  S&M  — Sales & Marketing: salespeople, advertising, commissions, customer acquisition.  G&A  — General & Administrative: executives, finance, legal, HR, offices. (S&M + G&A are often reported together as  SG&A .)
Interpretation: Cost of Revenue vs OpEx:  Cost of Revenue scales with each unit sold (direct). OpEx is the cost of the organisation — it can grow slower than revenue, which creates operating leverage.
Cautions: DO NOT subtract Cost of Revenue twice.  Gross Profit already has Cost of Revenue removed. Some data sites show “Total operating expenses” that  includes  COGS — check before using it.
Where to find: Lines between Gross Profit and Operating Income.

Handbook formula: Operating Income = Gross Profit − Operating Expenses
Meaning: Profit from the company’s core business after all operating costs,  before  interest and taxes. It measures how profitable the operations are, regardless of how the company is financed.
Interpretation: Strictly,  EBIT  (Earnings Before Interest and Taxes) also includes non-operating income; in practice the two are often used interchangeably.
Cautions: One-off items (restructuring, impairments, legal settlements) can distort it. Check “adjusted” figures against GAAP.

Handbook formula: Net Income = Operating Income − Interest ± Other Income/Expenses − Taxes
Meaning: What remains after  operating expenses ,  interest ,  taxes , and  other income/expenses . The “bottom line”, attributable to shareholders.
Interpretation: Net income is  accounting profit , not cash. It includes non-cash items (depreciation, stock-based compensation) and timing differences (receivables).
Cautions: One-off gains (selling a business, investment gains, tax benefits) can inflate it.  Profit ≠ Cash Flow.
Where to find: Last main line of the income statement.

Meaning: Gross Margin shows how much of a company’s revenue remains after paying the direct costs required to produce its products or services.
Interpretation: For every $100 in revenue, the company retains $60 after direct production/service costs. High gross margin often signals pricing power or a differentiated product.
Cautions: Different industries naturally have very different Gross Margins. A supermarket (~25%) and a software company (~75%) should not be compared directly.
Related cards: gross-profit, operating-margin, revenue-mix, ev-revenue, profitable-growth, backlog-quality

Meaning: The share of revenue left as operating profit after  all  operating costs — direct costs  and  R&D, sales and administration.
Interpretation: Gross vs Operating margin:  gross margin shows product economics; operating margin shows the economics of the whole company. A company can have  high gross margin but low or negative operating margin  if it invests heavily in R&D, sales or infrastructure.
Cautions: Gross Margin ≠ Operating Margin.  One-off charges, capitalised costs, or excluding stock-based compensation (“adjusted”) can flatter it.
Related cards: operating-income, operating-leverage, gross-margin, net-margin, fcf-margin, ev-revenue, profitable-growth, operating-margin-trend

AVGO coverage: No direct company-specific mapping; use handbook guidance and add your own evidence.
Meaning: The effect of fixed costs: when a large part of costs is fixed, revenue growth produces  proportionally larger  growth in operating income — margins expand. It also works in reverse when revenue falls.
Interpretation: Revenue grew 20% but operating income more than doubled. This is why investors tolerate low margins in scaling businesses. Negative operating leverage occurs when operating expenses grow faster than revenue and squeeze Operating Margin, other things equal. Check Gross Margin as well: revenue outgrowing operating expenses alone does not guarantee better margins.
Cautions: Expected operating leverage often fails to appear if the company keeps raising spending.
Where to find: Observed over several years of income statements.
Additional guidance: Revenue ↑  Operating Expenses ↑ more slowly  Operating Margin ↑ (assuming stable Gross Margin)   Illustrative path with 60% Gross Margin; amounts in $m. Expenses keep rising while losses turn into profits. Meaning: The share of revenue that ends up as net income for shareholders.
Interpretation: The company keeps $5 of net profit for every $100 of revenue.
Cautions: Affected by interest, taxes, one-off gains and losses — less “pure” than operating margin.

AVGO coverage: No direct company-specific mapping; use handbook guidance and add your own evidence.
Meaning: Net income follows  accrual accounting : revenue is recorded when earned and costs when incurred — not when cash moves. So a  profitable company can have weak cash flow  (customers haven’t paid, inventory piling up, heavy CapEx), and a company can  temporarily generate cash despite weak earnings  (customers prepay, suppliers paid later, large non-cash charges).
Interpretation: Over many years, good businesses convert most of their net income into free cash flow. Persistent gaps need an explanation.
Cautions: Net income consistently above operating cash flow can signal aggressive accounting (receivables growing faster than sales). FCF that ignores SBC overstates owner cash.
Where to find: Reconciliation at the top of the Cash Flow Statement.
Related cards: working-capital, ocf, fcf, net-income, receivables, payables, earnings-quality
Additional guidance:
Item  Beginner explanation  Cash vs profit
           Depreciation   An old equipment purchase is expensed gradually over its life. The expense reduces profit, but no cash leaves today (it left when the asset was bought).  Cash > Profit
           Accounts Receivable   You sold on credit: revenue and profit are booked, but the customer hasn’t paid yet.  Cash < Profit
           Accounts Payable   You received goods but haven’t paid the supplier yet — the cost is booked, cash is still in the bank.  Cash > Profit
           Working Capital   The cash tied up in day-to-day operations (inventory + receivables − payables). When it grows, it absorbs cash.  Either way
           Stock-Based Compensation   Employees paid in shares: an expense with no cash out — but it dilutes shareholders. It is a real cost.  Cash > Profit
           CapEx   Buying equipment is cash out today, but only reaches the income statement slowly as depreciation.  Cash < Profit

AVGO coverage: No direct company-specific mapping; use handbook guidance and add your own evidence.
Handbook formula: Working Capital = Current Assets − Current Liabilities
Meaning: The money tied up in running the business day to day. Accounting definition: current assets − current liabilities. Operating version: receivables + inventory − payables.
Interpretation: An  increase  in working capital uses cash (reduces operating cash flow); a decrease releases cash.
Cautions: One-time working-capital releases can make a single year’s cash flow look unusually strong.
Related cards: profit-vs-cash, current-ratio, receivables, inventory, payables, earnings-quality

AVGO coverage: No direct company-specific mapping; use handbook guidance and add your own evidence.
Meaning: Shows the actual cash coming in and going out, split into three sections:
Interpretation: A healthy mature company: strongly positive OCF, negative investing (reinvesting), negative financing (returning cash / repaying debt).
Cautions: Positive financing cash flow every year means the company depends on outside money.
Additional guidance:
Operating Cash Flow (OCF)  Cash from normal business operations.   Cash collected from customers  Paid to suppliers & employees  Interest & taxes paid
          Investing Cash Flow  Spending on (or selling) long-term assets.   CapEx: factories, servers, equipment  Acquisitions  Buying/selling investments
          Financing Cash Flow  Cash to/from owners and lenders.   Borrowing / repaying debt  Issuing shares  Buybacks  Dividends

Handbook formula: OCF ≈ Net Income + Depreciation & Amortization + SBC ± Change in Working Capital
Meaning: The cash a company generates from its normal operations during a period. It starts from net income, adds back non-cash expenses (depreciation, SBC), and adjusts for working-capital changes.
Interpretation: Strong, growing OCF (above net income) suggests high-quality earnings and a business that funds itself.
Cautions: OCF can be boosted temporarily by delaying supplier payments or selling receivables. SBC is added back even though it dilutes owners.
Where to find: “Net cash provided by operating activities” in the Cash Flow Statement.

Meaning: Cash spent buying or upgrading long-lived assets:  factories, servers, data centres, machinery, vehicles, infrastructure .  Maintenance CapEx  — needed just to keep the existing business running (replacing worn-out assets).  Growth CapEx  — spending to expand capacity and future revenue.
Interpretation: Growth investment can reduce current FCF below a no-growth cash-generation estimate. Do not remove that spending while retaining the future growth it supports.
Cautions: High CapEx is not automatically bad  — the company may be investing in future growth. The maintenance/growth split is often an estimate. Depreciation allocates historical costs; inflation, technology changes, and deferred upkeep can make it a poor estimate of required maintenance.
Where to find: Investing section of the Cash Flow Statement (shown as a negative number).
Related cards: maintenance-capex, owner-earnings, fcf, roic, ebitda, cfs, ppe, capex-efficiency, profitable-growth, invested-capital

Meaning: The cash generated after paying for the investment needed to maintain and grow the business — the cash truly available to owners.
Interpretation: Investors care because FCF is what a company can use to:  reinvest ,  pay debt ,  buy back shares ,  pay dividends ,  acquire companies , or  hold cash . A business is ultimately worth the FCF it will generate (see DCF).
Cautions: FCF ignores stock-based compensation (a real cost). Cutting CapEx raises FCF short term but may hurt growth. FCF must be understood in the context of growth investment.
Where to find: Calculated from the Cash Flow Statement.
Related cards: fcf-margin, fcf-yield, dcf-intro, profit-vs-cash, cfs, ocf, capex, ebitda, price-fcf, owner-earnings, interest-coverage, ev-revenue, profitable-growth, backlog-quality, capex-efficiency

Meaning: Free cash flow as a percentage of revenue.
Interpretation: For every $100 of sales, $12 becomes free cash. Compare with operating margin: much lower FCF margin → heavy CapEx or working capital; higher → strong cash conversion (e.g. customer prepayments).
Cautions: Lumpy CapEx or working capital can distort a single year — look at multi-year averages.
Where to find: Calculated: Cash Flow Statement + Income Statement.

Meaning: Everything the company owns or controls that is expected to bring future economic benefit. Split into  current  (turn into cash within ~1 year) and  long-term .
Cautions: Assets are mostly recorded at historical cost, not current value. Goodwill can be large and later written down.
Where to find: Top half (or left side) of the Balance Sheet.
Additional guidance: Current Assets   Cash, accounts receivable, inventory, short-term investments     Long-Term Assets   PP&E, goodwill & intangibles, long-term investments, lease assets

Meaning: Assets that will be converted to cash or used up within about one year: cash, receivables, inventory, prepaid expenses, short-term investments.
Cautions: Not all current assets are equally liquid — obsolete inventory or doubtful receivables may never become cash.
Related cards: current-ratio, cash, receivables, inventory, assets, ncav

Meaning: Money in the bank and very liquid, low-risk investments (Treasury bills, money-market funds). Many analysts add short-term investments too.
Interpretation: Why it matters:  stability — cash lets a company survive downturns and invest when others can’t. Valuation — cash belongs to shareholders, so it is  subtracted  in Enterprise Value and  added  back in the DCF equity bridge.
Cautions: Some cash may be trapped abroad, restricted, or needed for operations (e.g. customer funds held by payment companies).

AVGO coverage: 11 reported records (includes unavailable rows); Discussed in steps 1
Meaning: Amounts customers owe for goods/services already delivered but not yet paid for.
Interpretation: Receivables growing much faster than revenue may signal looser credit terms, collection problems, or aggressive revenue recognition.
Cautions: Rising receivables make profit look better than cash.

Meaning: Raw materials, work-in-progress and finished goods not yet sold.
Interpretation: Inventory ties up cash. Rising faster than sales can foreshadow discounts and write-downs.
Cautions: Obsolete or fashion-sensitive inventory may be worth far less than its book value.

Meaning: Physical long-term assets used to operate the business, shown net of accumulated depreciation.
Interpretation: CapEx increases PP&E; depreciation reduces it. Capital-intensive businesses have large PP&E relative to revenue.
Cautions: Recorded at historical cost less depreciation — may differ greatly from replacement or market value.

Meaning: Obligations the company owes: suppliers, lenders, employees, tax authorities, customers who prepaid. Split into  current  (due within ~1 year) and  long-term .
Cautions: Not all liabilities are bad: deferred revenue is cash customers already paid.
Where to find: Bottom half of the Balance Sheet.
Related cards: current-liabilities, debt, equity, assets, ncav, deferred-revenue
Additional guidance: Current Liabilities   Accounts payable, short-term debt, accrued expenses, deferred revenue     Long-Term Liabilities   Long-term debt, lease liabilities, pensions, deferred taxes

Meaning: Obligations due within about a year: accounts payable, short-term debt and current portion of long-term debt, accrued expenses, deferred revenue.
Cautions: Large debt maturities inside current liabilities can be a refinancing risk.

Meaning: Bills from suppliers the company has received but not yet paid.
Interpretation: Paying suppliers later keeps cash longer — a free source of financing for companies with bargaining power.
Cautions: Stretching payables can boost cash flow temporarily — it can’t continue forever.

Meaning: Borrowed money (bank loans, bonds) that must be repaid with interest.  Short-Term Debt  — due within a year (including the current portion of long-term debt).  Long-Term Debt  — due after more than a year.
Interpretation: Interest burden:  interest payments reduce profit and cash.  Maturity risk:  debt must be repaid or refinanced when due — dangerous if it comes due when credit markets are closed or the business is weak.
Cautions: Leases and other obligations behave like debt but may not be included in “debt” on data sites.
Where to find: Current and long-term liabilities; debt maturity note in the 10-K.
Related cards: net-debt, debt-ebitda, enterprise-value, risk-factors, liabilities, net-cash, invested-capital

AVGO coverage: No direct company-specific mapping; use handbook guidance and add your own evidence.
Meaning: Cash minus total debt. If positive, the company has more cash than debt.
Interpretation: Positive net cash means the company could repay all its debt today and still have cash left — financial flexibility for downturns, buybacks or acquisitions. Cash > Debt means Net Cash. EV = Market Cap − Net Cash: $20B equity with $3B Net Cash implies $17B EV.
Cautions: Some cash may be needed to run the business or be trapped abroad.

Meaning: Total debt minus cash. Used when debt exceeds cash.
Interpretation: Analysts care more about net debt than gross debt because cash could be used to repay debt. Two companies each with $10B of debt are very different if one has $9B of cash. Debt > Cash means Net Debt. EV = Market Cap + Net Debt: $20B equity with $8B Net Debt implies $28B EV.
Cautions: Assumes all cash is available to repay debt, which may not be true.

Handbook formula: Current Ratio = Current Assets / Current Liabilities
Meaning: Measures whether short-term assets cover short-term obligations.
Interpretation: 2.0 means $2 of current assets for every $1 of current liabilities.
Cautions: Limitations:  inventory may not be sellable; receivables may not be collected; subscription companies often run below 1.0 safely because of deferred revenue; it says nothing about long-term debt.

Meaning: What would be left for shareholders if all assets were sold at book value and all liabilities paid.
Interpretation: Grows with retained profits and share issuance; shrinks with losses, dividends and buybacks.
Cautions: Large buybacks can make equity small or even negative in excellent businesses.

Handbook formula:
Book Value = Assets − Liabilities
Price / Book = Market Cap / Book Value
Meaning: The accounting value of shareholders’ equity on the balance sheet. Per share: Equity / Shares.
Interpretation: Book Value ≠ Market Value.  Book value reflects historical accounting; market value reflects expectations about future cash flows. Asset-light businesses (software, brands) trade far above book.
Cautions: Most useful for banks and asset-heavy firms; nearly meaningless for many tech companies.

Hebrew title: רווח לפני ריבית, מסים, פחת והפחתות
Meaning: Operating profit before deducting depreciation and amortization (and before interest and taxes).
Interpretation: Analysts  use it to compare businesses with different debt, tax and depreciation policies.  Lenders  use it to size debt and set covenants (Debt/EBITDA). It is useful for comparing businesses because it is capital-structure neutral.
Cautions: EBITDA ≠ CASH FLOW.  It ignores CapEx, working capital, interest and taxes. It can make  capital-intensive businesses look much better  than they are — depreciation reflects equipment that must be replaced.
Where to find: Calculated (sometimes reported as “Adjusted EBITDA” — check what’s excluded).

Meaning: A rough measure of leverage: how many years of EBITDA it would take to repay all debt.
Interpretation: Conceptually:  1x  — debt equals one year of EBITDA, light.  2x  — two years.  5x  — five years of all EBITDA, heavy for most businesses. There are  no universal thresholds : stable utilities carry more debt safely than cyclical or fast-changing businesses.
Cautions: EBITDA ignores CapEx and can collapse in a downturn, so leverage can rise suddenly.
Where to find: Calculated from Balance Sheet + Income Statement.

Meaning: Operating profit after tax, calculated as if the company had no debt. It isolates the profit produced by the  operations .
Interpretation: Why NOPAT instead of Net Income for ROIC?  Net income is after interest, so it depends on how much debt the company has. ROIC measures return to  all  capital (debt + equity), so the numerator must be before interest — NOPAT.
Cautions: Use a realistic (effective/cash) tax rate; one-off items in operating income distort it.

Handbook formula: Simple version:  Invested Capital = Shareholders’ Equity + Debt − Cash
Meaning: The amount of capital invested in the operating business — the money shareholders and lenders have put in to buy the factories, equipment, inventory and acquisitions the business runs on.
Interpretation: There are several detailed ways analysts calculate it — e.g. the operating approach: Net PP&E + Net Working Capital (+ Goodwill & Intangibles). Different methods give different ROICs; be consistent.
Cautions: Goodwill from acquisitions, buybacks (reduce equity), and negative working capital can make it tiny or distorted.
Related cards: roic, equity, debt, ppe, nopat, profitable-growth, capex

Meaning: Measures how efficiently the business converts invested capital into after-tax operating profit.
Interpretation: The business generates approximately  $0.20  of after-tax operating profit for every  $1  of invested capital.  Consistently  high ROIC (e.g. 15%+ for many years) is strong evidence of a moat and a high-quality business — competitors would normally compete those returns away.
Cautions: Accounting differences, acquisitions (goodwill), unusual capital structure, and one-time items can all distort ROIC. One great year proves nothing.
Where to find: Calculated from Income Statement + Balance Sheet.
Related cards: nopat, invested-capital, wacc, moat, capex, incremental-roic, ev-revenue, profitable-growth, capex-efficiency, embedded-expectations
Additional guidance: ROIC vs WACC    ROIC > WACC  — generally creates economic value.   ROIC < WACC  — may destroy economic value.   ROIC ≈ WACC  — approximately earns its Cost of Capital.   ROIC − WACC Spread  Value Creation Spread = ROIC − WACC  ROIC 18% − WACC 9% = +9 percentage points. A positive spread is generally desirable.  Check sustainable, forward-looking incremental returns. Historical average ROIC can hide weak new projects.

AVGO coverage: Discussed in steps 2, 4; Model assumption: WACC 9.00%
Handbook formula: WACC = (Equity Weight × Cost of Equity) + (Debt Weight × Cost of Debt × (1 − Tax Rate))
Meaning: WACC is the blended required return of the providers financing a business: primarily equity investors and debt investors. It is the typical Discount Rate for FCFF.
Interpretation: Use market-value equity and debt weights that sum to 100%. Interest may reduce taxable income, so the debt cost is adjusted for the usable tax benefit. The adjustment assumes interest deductions can be used.
Cautions: WACC is an estimate, not a universal fixed hurdle. Deduction limits or tax losses can reduce the usable tax benefit. Use cost of equity for FCFE. Growth creates value only when incremental returns exceed the appropriate cost of capital.
Related cards: roic, cost-of-equity, discount-rate, incremental-roic, profitable-growth, required-return, opportunity-cost, present-value, dcf-intro, fcff

Handbook formula: Cost of Equity = Risk-free Rate + Beta × Equity Risk Premium
Meaning: The cost of equity is the expected return that investors require to hold the company’s shares. Shareholders are paid last and carry the most risk, so the cost of equity is higher than the cost of debt. Most analysts estimate it with the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM).
Interpretation: Risk-free rate: the yield on a long-term government bond in the same currency as the cash flows. Beta: how much the stock moved with the market in the past; a beta of 1.0 means average market risk. Equity risk premium: the extra return investors require from stocks over government bonds, commonly 4–6% for the US market.
Cautions: Beta comes from past prices and changes with the period and index you choose. A single stock’s beta is noisy, so many analysts use the average beta of similar companies, adjusted for debt. CAPM ignores risks specific to the company, such as small size or customer concentration. Small input changes move a DCF value a lot, so check the sensitivity table. Match the currency and inflation of the risk-free rate to the cash flows.
Where to find: Estimated by you (not reported). Risk-free rate: government bond yields. Beta: data providers or your own regression. Equity risk premium: published surveys and estimates (for example, Aswath Damodaran).
Related cards: wacc, discount-rate, required-return, fcfe, opportunity-cost, sensitivity
Additional guidance: Risk-free Rate  + Beta × Equity Risk Premium  Cost of Equity  Discount rate for FCFE, or an input to WACC for FCFF

Meaning: The total number of shares currently issued and held by investors (excluding treasury shares the company bought back).
Interpretation: Used to convert company-level numbers into per-share numbers (EPS, value per share) and to calculate Market Cap.
Cautions: Use  diluted  shares for valuation. The cover page of the 10-K/10-Q shows the latest count.
Where to find: Bottom of the Income Statement (weighted average) and 10-K cover page.

AVGO coverage: No direct company-specific mapping; use handbook guidance and add your own evidence.
Meaning: The weighted-average number of shares actually outstanding during the period. Used for  Basic EPS .
Cautions: Ignores options, RSUs and convertibles that will likely become shares.

AVGO coverage: 10 reported records (includes unavailable rows); Discussed in steps 3
Meaning: Basic shares plus all shares that could be created from stock options, restricted stock units (RSUs), warrants and convertible bonds. Used for  Diluted EPS  and fair value per share.
Interpretation: The more conservative and correct denominator for valuation.
Cautions: Even “diluted” may understate future dilution if the company keeps granting large stock compensation.

Handbook formula: Annual dilution = (Shares this year − Shares last year) / Shares last year
Meaning: When a company issues new shares (to employees via stock compensation, to raise money, or for acquisitions), each existing share owns a smaller percentage of the company.
Interpretation: A company can grow while existing shareholders are diluted: the company got bigger, but your slice grew much less.
Cautions: Companies may offset dilution with buybacks — check how much cash buybacks really consume.
Related cards: diluted-shares, eps, shares-outstanding, owner-earnings, capital-allocation, management-incentives

Meaning: Net income divided by the number of shares: the profit attributable to each share. Reported as Basic and Diluted EPS.
Interpretation: Per-share metrics matter because shareholders own shares, not the company. EPS growth is what ultimately drives share price over time.
Cautions: Buybacks raise EPS without business improvement; “adjusted EPS” often excludes real costs like SBC.

Handbook formula: Market Cap = Share Price × Shares Outstanding
Meaning: The market value of the company’s equity — what the stock market currently charges for all of its shares.
Interpretation: Share price by itself tells almost nothing  about whether a stock is cheap. A $500 stock with 100M shares ($50B) is “smaller” than a $10 stock with 10B shares ($100B). Market Cap values equity, not the underlying operating business. Compare share counts over time: issuance and buybacks change Market Cap even with an unchanged Share Price.
Cautions: Use current shares outstanding for current Market Cap, not weighted-average diluted EPS shares. Track issuance, buybacks and potential dilution separately. Compare the same date for price and shares.
Related cards: enterprise-value, pe, fcf-yield, book-value, equity-value, price-sales

Handbook formula:
P/E = Market Cap / Net Income
P/E = Share Price / EPS
Meaning: How many dollars investors pay for each dollar of the company’s annual earnings.
Interpretation: P/E 20x means investors currently pay ~$20 for every $1 of annual earnings (earnings yield = 1/20 = 5%).  Growth and quality matter:  a fast-growing, high-ROIC company deserves a higher P/E because its future earnings will be much larger.
Cautions: Low P/E ≠ automatically cheap  (declining business, peak-cycle earnings, one-off gains).  High P/E ≠ automatically expensive  (fast growth, temporarily depressed earnings). Meaningless when earnings are negative.

Meaning: An approximation of the value of the whole operating business, independent of how it is financed.
Interpretation: Imagine buying the whole company: you pay the market cap, but you also  take on its debt  (you must repay it → add) and you  get its cash  (it reduces your real cost → subtract).  Market Cap = Equity Value. Enterprise Value = approximate value of the operating enterprise.  EV approximates operating business value and helps compare different capital structures. Net Cash can put EV below Market Cap; high Net Debt can put it significantly above Market Cap.
Cautions: Market Cap ≠ Enterprise Value.  A precise EV also adds preferred stock, minority interests and often leases.
Related cards: market-cap, ev-ebitda, dcf-ev, cash, debt, net-debt, ev-revenue

Meaning: Values the whole business relative to its EBITDA.
Interpretation: Why pair EV with EBITDA?  EBITDA is earned before interest, so it belongs to  all  capital providers (debt and equity) — matching EV, which also includes debt. Useful for comparing companies with different leverage and in M&A.
Cautions: Limitations:  EBITDA ignores CapEx, so capital-intensive businesses look cheap. Cross-check with EV/EBIT or Price/FCF. “Adjusted EBITDA” may exclude real costs.

AVGO coverage: No direct company-specific mapping; use handbook guidance and add your own evidence.
Handbook formula: Price / FCF = Market Cap / Free Cash Flow
Meaning: How many dollars investors pay for each dollar of annual free cash flow.
Interpretation: Like P/E but based on cash rather than accounting profit. 20x means paying $20 for $1 of annual FCF.
Cautions: One year of FCF can be lumpy (CapEx timing, working capital). SBC isn’t deducted.

Handbook formula: FCF Yield = Free Cash Flow / Market Cap
Meaning: Annual free cash flow as a percentage of market value — the cash “yield” you get at today’s price.
Interpretation: For every $100 of market value the company generates ~$10 of FCF per year.  Inverse of Price/FCF:  10% yield ⇔ 10x P/FCF; 4% ⇔ 25x.
Cautions: A high yield with shrinking FCF is a trap; a low yield can be fine with strong growth.

AVGO coverage: No direct company-specific mapping; use handbook guidance and add your own evidence.
Meaning: The central tradeoff of stock valuation: a stock that gives a lot of cash relative to its price today vs one that gives little today but may grow much larger.
Interpretation: A  provides much more cash relative to today’s valuation.  B  provides less current cash but potentially much higher future cash —  if  growth continues. B overtakes A in year 5. Neither metric (yield or growth) should be viewed alone; a DCF combines both.
Cautions: High expected growth is already priced in; if it disappoints, the low-yield stock can fall a lot.
Related cards: fcf-yield, dcf-intro, pe, embedded-expectations, required-return, opportunity-cost
Additional guidance:
FCF Yield  FCF Growth  FCF per $100 — year 0  Year 5  Year 10
           Company A   10%  3%  $10.00  $11.59  $13.44
           Company B   4%  25%  $4.00  $12.21  $37.25

AVGO coverage: No direct company-specific mapping; use handbook guidance and add your own evidence.
Meaning: Money today is worth more than the same amount received in the future, when the required return is positive.
Interpretation: Today’s money can earn investment returns. Waiting has an opportunity cost; inflation reduces purchasing power, and future cash flows carry risk and uncertainty. DCF translates those future cash flows into today’s value.
Cautions: Match nominal cash flows with nominal rates and real cash flows with real rates. Do not deduct inflation twice.

AVGO coverage: No direct company-specific mapping; use handbook guidance and add your own evidence.
Handbook formula: Value = Σ FCFₜ / (1 + r)ᵗ  +  Terminal Value / (1 + r)ᴺ
Meaning: A valuation method that estimates what a business is worth today by forecasting its future free cash flows and discounting them back to the present.
Interpretation: The output is only as good as the assumptions. Use it to understand  what you must believe  for the stock to be cheap — and what the current price implies.
Cautions: DCF is based on assumptions, not certainty.  Small changes in growth, r or g move the value a lot.
Related cards: present-value, terminal-value, sensitivity, fcff, fcfe, reverse-dcf, fcf, growth-vs-valuation, time-value-money, wacc, profitable-growth, dcf-ev, equity-value, fair-value-per-share

AVGO coverage: No direct company-specific mapping; use handbook guidance and add your own evidence.
Handbook formula:
PV = Future Cash Flow / (1 + r)^t
PV = Present Value · r = Discount Rate per period · t = Number of periods
Meaning: What a future amount of money is worth today. Money today is worth more than money later because it can be invested, and the future is uncertain.
Interpretation: At a 10% required return, receiving $90.91 today is equivalent to $100 in a year. Present Value converts future money into today’s economic value. Use the calculator below; set Years to 10 to reproduce the $38.55 example.
Cautions: The further away the cash flow and the higher r, the less it is worth today.

AVGO coverage: No direct company-specific mapping; use handbook guidance and add your own evidence.
Meaning: Future Value compounds today’s money forward at an assumed rate of return.
Interpretation: Compounding asks what today’s money will be worth in the future. Discounting reverses the direction: what is future money worth today?
Cautions: The assumed return is not guaranteed. Match the rate and period; these examples use annual compounding without fees or taxes.
Additional guidance: Compounding vs Discounting    Compounding  Present → Future: What will today’s money be worth? PV × (1 + r)^t = FV     Discounting  Future → Present: What is future money worth today? FV / (1 + r)^t = PV

Meaning: The minimum expected return investors require for time, risk and opportunity cost.
Interpretation: Higher perceived risk generally increases the required return. Match the required return to the claims and cash flows being valued.
Cautions: A required return is a hurdle, not a promised or realized return. An arbitrary target does not establish a company’s WACC.
Additional guidance: Risk  Required Return  Discount Rate  Valuation

Meaning: The annual rate used to convert future cash into today’s value. It reflects the time value of money and risk — riskier businesses get higher discount rates. Use WACC for FCFF and the cost of equity for FCFE. The Discount Rate is the required return used to calculate Present Value.
Interpretation: Discount Rate ↑ → Valuation ↓. Discount Rate ↓ → Valuation ↑.
Cautions: Small changes in the rate can materially change DCF value. Match the rate to cash-flow risk, currency and inflation assumptions.
Related cards: cost-of-equity, wacc, present-value, sensitivity, terminal-value, fcfe, opportunity-cost, future-value, required-return
Additional guidance: Higher Risk  Higher Required Return  Higher Discount Rate  Lower Present Value   The $100 cash flow did not change. Only the required return changed. Higher rates reduce the Present Value of positive future cash flows; lower rates increase it.  Try both rates in the Present Value calculator

Handbook formula:
Terminal Value = FCF next year / (r − g)

r = Discount Rate · g = Terminal Growth Rate
PV of TV = TV / (1 + r)ᴺ
Meaning: We cannot forecast a company year by year forever, so after the explicit forecast (e.g. 10 years) we assume FCF grows at a modest constant rate  g  forever and capture all of it in one number.
Interpretation: Terminal value often represents  60–80%  of a DCF’s total value, because it covers every year after the forecast — that is why DCFs are so sensitive to r and g.
Cautions: r must be greater than g  — otherwise the formula breaks (division by zero or a negative number). g should not exceed long-run economic growth (~2–4%).

AVGO coverage: No direct company-specific mapping; use handbook guidance and add your own evidence.
Handbook formula: Enterprise Value = PV of Forecast FCF + PV of Terminal Value
Meaning: The value of the whole operating business implied by your DCF.
Interpretation: Discount FCFF, the cash flow available to all capital providers, at WACC to estimate operating enterprise value. Discounting FCFE at the cost of equity instead gives equity value.
Cautions: Check what share comes from terminal value.
Related cards: equity-value, enterprise-value, fcff, fcfe, terminal-value, dcf-intro

AVGO coverage: No direct company-specific mapping; use handbook guidance and add your own evidence.
Handbook formula: Equity Value = Enterprise Value − Debt + Cash
Meaning: The part of enterprise value that belongs to shareholders, after lenders are repaid and cash is added.
Interpretation: Comparable to Market Cap. If your equity value is above the market cap, the stock may be undervalued (according to your assumptions).
Cautions: Include all debt-like items (leases, preferred stock, minority interests) for precision.

Handbook formula:
Fair Value Per Share = Equity Value / Diluted Shares Outstanding
Upside / Downside = Fair Value / Current Price − 1
Meaning: Your estimate of what one share is worth.
Interpretation: Compare with the current price — but as a  range  (bear/base/bull), not one number.
Cautions: Use diluted shares; false precision ($26.37) is a warning sign.

AVGO coverage: No direct company-specific mapping; use handbook guidance and add your own evidence.
Meaning: Re-running the DCF across a grid of assumptions (typically discount rate × terminal growth) to see a  range  of values instead of one magical number.
Interpretation: A good investment often has limited downside in the bear case and meaningful upside in base/bull. Also ask in reverse:  what assumptions are already priced into the stock?
Cautions: Valuation should be a range, not a single magical number.
Related cards: terminal-value, discount-rate, dcf-intro, fair-value-per-share, margin-of-safety, reverse-dcf, embedded-expectations
Additional guidance:
Discount Rate ↑  → Valuation ↓   Discount Rate ↓  → Valuation ↑   Terminal Growth ↑  → Valuation ↑   Terminal Growth ↓  → Valuation ↓
           Bear case  Lower growth, lower margins, higher discount rate, conservative terminal assumptions.    Base case  Most reasonable assumptions.    Bull case  Higher growth, higher margins, operating leverage.

Meaning: A concise argument (a few sentences) explaining  what you believe that the market doesn’t , why it matters for value, and what will make the market recognise it.
Interpretation: A good thesis is specific and falsifiable: “Margins will expand from 10% to 18% as data-centre utilisation rises; the market prices in 12%.”
Cautions: “Great company” is not a thesis. If you can’t say why the market is wrong, you probably don’t have an edge.
Additional guidance: 1 Business   2 Moat   3 Growth Drivers   4 Financial Quality   5 Capital Efficiency   6 Valuation   7 Catalysts   8 Risks   9 Bear Case   10 Base Case   11 Bull Case   12 Thesis Invalidation

Meaning: 3–10 specific, measurable conditions — written before you invest — that would mean your thesis is broken.
Interpretation: When a condition triggers, re-underwrite from scratch: would you buy this stock today at this price?
Cautions: Moving the goalposts after the fact (“it’s only temporary”) is confirmation bias in action.

Handbook formula: Margin of Safety = (Estimated Value − Price) / Estimated Value
Meaning: A purchase price below conservatively estimated intrinsic value leaves room for some errors in your assumptions. The protection depends on the quality of that estimate.
Interpretation: A 30% discount to value is different from 30% upside from price. Use a range of values and investigate the downside assumptions.
Cautions: An optimistic valuation can manufacture an apparent discount. No fixed percentage guarantees protection.
Where to find: Your valuation model and the current share price.

Handbook formula: Owner Earnings ≈ Net Income + D&A − Maintenance CapEx − Required Increase in Operating Working Capital
Meaning: An estimate of cash earning power after the reinvestment needed to preserve current operations and competitive position. It requires judgment about maintenance spending and working capital.
Interpretation: This simplified example assumes no other adjustments. Reconcile unusual gains, losses, and other non-cash items individually. Keep stock-based compensation as an economic cost.
Cautions: If you start from operating cash flow, working-capital changes are already included. Do not subtract them twice or exclude investment while retaining the growth it funds.
Where to find: Financial statements, asset notes, and your maintenance estimates.

AVGO coverage: No direct company-specific mapping; use handbook guidance and add your own evidence.
Meaning: Spending needed to sustain the existing business, including necessary replacements and upgrades. The maintenance/growth split is often an estimate rather than a reported accounting line.
Interpretation: Build a range from asset age, replacement costs, replacement cycles, capacity, and required upgrades. Compare management’s estimates with spending history.
Cautions: Depreciation allocates historical costs. Inflation, technology, asset age, and deferred upkeep can make it a poor estimate of current maintenance needs.
Where to find: PP&E notes, capital-spending disclosures, operating data, and management commentary.

Handbook formula: Adjusted Earnings = Reported Earnings − Unusual Gains + Unusual Costs (all after tax)
Meaning: An estimate of repeatable earning power. Remove genuinely unusual gains and costs symmetrically, then consider whether current demand, prices, and margins are sustainable.
Interpretation: The arithmetic is a starting point. A cyclical company can still have unusually high adjusted earnings at peak demand.
Cautions: Repeated restructuring charges are not automatically exceptional. A historical average can also mislead after structural business changes.
Where to find: Income statement, footnotes, and financial history.
Related cards: cyclicality, earnings-quality, pe, owner-earnings, value-trap, operating-margin-trend

Meaning: Management chooses between reinvestment, acquisitions, debt repayment, dividends, buybacks, and retaining cash. Judge the results relative to risk and available alternatives.
Interpretation: Compare the likely value created by each use of funds. A larger company or higher EPS does not necessarily mean better allocation.
Cautions: Buybacks can destroy value when shares are overpriced or liquidity is needed. Acquisition growth can conceal poor returns.
Where to find: Cash flow statement, acquisition notes, shareholder letters, and proxy disclosures.
Related cards: incremental-roic, management-incentives, opportunity-cost, dilution, fcfe, capex-efficiency, profitable-growth

Meaning: A stock can look cheap on past profits or recorded assets while earning power, asset recoverability, or shareholder value deteriorates. The apparent discount may never have represented true value.
Interpretation: Investigate why the price is low. Separate temporary setbacks from lasting damage, and identify evidence that would disprove your recovery assumptions.
Cautions: A missing catalyst or a long period of undervaluation alone does not establish a value trap. A catalyst also cannot repair weak economics by itself.
Where to find: Multi-year statements, competitive evidence, and your thesis review.
Related cards: catalysts, normalized-earnings, maintenance-capex, invalidation, margin-of-safety, permanent-capital-loss, liquidation-value, ncav

Handbook formula: Incremental ROIC ≈ Change in NOPAT / Change in Invested Capital
Meaning: Estimate how effectively a business turns new investment into additional after-tax operating profit. Use periods long enough for the investment to produce results.
Interpretation: Compare incremental returns with the cost of capital. High returns on old assets do not prove new projects will earn similar returns.
Cautions: Acquisitions, inflation, timing, and write-downs distort the calculation. A near-zero or negative capital change makes the ratio hard to interpret.
Related cards: roic, wacc, capital-allocation, reverse-dcf, capex-efficiency, profitable-growth

Meaning: Start with market value and solve for an assumption, such as revenue growth, that makes the discounted cash flows match it. Hold other assumptions explicit.
Interpretation: Ask whether the required growth, margins, and reinvestment are plausible. Repeat with different discount rates and terminal assumptions. Test required Revenue Growth, Operating Margin and Free Cash Flow while explicitly fixing Terminal Growth, reinvestment and ROIC assumptions. Change one assumption at a time; many combinations can support the same value.
Cautions: Many combinations can explain one price. The implied growth rate is conditional, not an observable market forecast.
Where to find: Your DCF model and current market capitalization, debt, and cash.
Additional guidance: Traditional DCF:  Assumptions → Estimated Fair Value   Reverse DCF:  Current Market Value → Required Future Performance    Interactive Reverse DCF calculator — planned  Reserved for a future single-assumption solver. No automatic solution is calculated here yet.  Explore assumptions in the existing DCF calculator

Meaning: A common measure compares EBIT with interest expense to assess the earnings available to cover financing costs.
Interpretation: Test coverage under weaker earnings and higher borrowing costs. This ratio does not show whether the principal can be repaid.
Cautions: Zero interest expense makes this ratio undefined. Negative EBIT indicates earnings do not cover interest. EBITDA-based coverage is a different measure.

Meaning: A company may need a new loan or bond issue when existing debt matures. New funding may be unavailable, more expensive, or subject to tighter conditions.
Interpretation: Map maturities against available liquidity, realistic cash generation, and committed credit facilities. Examine covenants and collateral.
Cautions: Undrawn facilities can have conditions. Restricted cash and optimistic asset-sale proceeds may not be available when needed.
Where to find: Debt footnotes, liquidity disclosures, and credit agreements.

Meaning: Assess whether profits depend on sustainable operations or on temporary events, estimates, and aggressive accounting. Reconcile profit with cash generation over time.
Interpretation: Look for evidence in revenue recognition, capitalization policies, reserves, and repeated adjustments. A warning signal starts an investigation; it is not proof of misconduct.
Cautions: High operating cash flow can come from delayed supplier payments or customer prepayments. Cash conversion alone does not establish earnings quality.
Where to find: Accounting policies, financial statements, and reconciliation notes.

English title: Free Cash Flow to the Firm
Handbook formula: FCFF = EBIT × (1 − Tax Rate) + D&A − CapEx − Increase in Non-cash Operating Working Capital
Meaning: Cash available to debt and equity providers together. An operating approach starts with after-tax operating profit and deducts reinvestment.
Interpretation: Discount FCFF at WACC to estimate operating business value. Then account for cash, debt, and other non-operating assets or claims to reach equity value.
Cautions: Reported OCF minus CapEx is not automatically FCFF because interest treatment can differ. This simplified formula assumes no other adjustments.

Handbook formula: FCFE = Net Income + D&A − CapEx − Increase in Non-cash Operating Working Capital + Net Borrowing
Meaning: Start with earnings after interest and taxes, adjust for reinvestment, and include borrowing less principal repayments.
Interpretation: Discount FCFE at the cost of equity to value the equity claim directly. Do not subtract debt again from that equity valuation.
Cautions: Match cash flows and discount rates. Adjust separately for omitted non-operating assets and other claims; avoid counting them twice.
Where to find: Equity cash-flow forecasts and financing schedules.
Related cards: cost-of-equity, fcff, discount-rate, capital-allocation, dcf-intro, dcf-ev

Meaning: Define where you understand how a business earns money, what can damage it, and which assumptions you can assess. Recognize the limits of that knowledge.
Interpretation: Write down what you know, what you infer, and what you cannot assess. Expand your knowledge through evidence rather than familiarity alone.
Cautions: Using a product or knowing an industry’s vocabulary does not establish valuation competence.
Where to find: Your research notes and decision checklist.

Meaning: Business failure, lasting economic damage, severe dilution, or paying too much can leave an investment unable to recover its original purchasing power.
Interpretation: Analyze how the investment could fail economically. A share-price decline may signal that risk, but does not by itself prove permanent damage.
Cautions: Low price volatility does not establish safety. Forced selling can turn a temporary decline into a realized loss.
Where to find: Scenario analysis and portfolio liquidity planning.

AVGO coverage: No direct company-specific mapping; use handbook guidance and add your own evidence.
Meaning: Compare an investment with realistic alternatives, including retaining liquidity. Consider risk, time, taxes, and confidence in the estimates. Capital invested in one company cannot simultaneously be invested elsewhere. The opportunity cost of capital reflects alternatives with comparable risk.
Interpretation: An investment can appear undervalued yet be less attractive than another available use of funds.
Cautions: Forecast precision is limited. Switching also has transaction costs and possible taxes.
Where to find: Your investment comparisons and management allocation decisions.
Related cards: capital-allocation, discount-rate, margin-of-safety, time-value-money, required-return, wacc, growth-vs-valuation

Meaning: Examine what managers are rewarded for and whether those rewards support lasting per-share value. Review targets, vesting periods, ownership, and governance.
Interpretation: Compare stated priorities with actual pay formulas and capital allocation. Consider minority shareholders as well as controlling owners.
Cautions: Large insider ownership can align interests but can also entrench control. Adjusted performance metrics may exclude real costs.
Where to find: Proxy statements, remuneration reports, and ownership disclosures.

Handbook formula: Common Tangible Book Value = Total Equity − Preferred Equity − Goodwill − Other Intangible Assets
Meaning: A balance-sheet measure that removes recorded goodwill and other intangibles from equity. For a common-share measure, also exclude preferred equity.
Interpretation: This can help assess some asset-heavy businesses and financial institutions. It does not measure the full economic value of a franchise.
Cautions: Tangible book value is not liquidation value. Recorded assets may require write-downs, and liabilities or disposal costs may exceed expectations.
Where to find: Balance sheet and goodwill, intangible-asset, and equity notes.

AVGO coverage: No direct company-specific mapping; use handbook guidance and add your own evidence.
Handbook formula: Common Equity Liquidation Value ≈ Asset Sale Proceeds − Liabilities − Preferred Claims − Closure Costs
Meaning: Estimate realizable asset proceeds, then deduct liabilities, senior claims, and closure costs. Distinguish orderly sales from distressed sales.
Interpretation: Use asset-specific recovery assumptions and allow for the time needed to sell assets. Investigate taxes, leases, pensions, and other obligations.
Cautions: Book values are not sale prices. Operating losses can consume assets while shareholders wait, and closure costs are uncertain.
Where to find: Asset notes, claim schedules, appraisals, and wind-down estimates.

Handbook formula: Common NCAV = Current Assets − Total Liabilities − Preferred Equity
Meaning: A conservative asset-screening measure that excludes long-term assets but deducts all liabilities. A stock below this measure is often called a net-net candidate.
Interpretation: Compare the measure with market capitalization, then examine asset recoverability and cash consumption. It is a research screen, not a purchase rule.
Cautions: Subtract all liabilities, not only current liabilities. NCAV can disappear through losses, poor allocation, or unrecoverable assets.

AVGO coverage: No direct company-specific mapping; use handbook guidance and add your own evidence.
Meaning: Equity market value per dollar of revenue. Useful when earnings are negative or temporarily depressed.
Interpretation: Compare the same revenue period and similar businesses. Two companies with identical P/S can deserve very different valuations because margins, reinvestment and risk differ.
Cautions: Does not account for debt or tell you whether sales are profitable. A low multiple is not proof of cheapness.

AVGO coverage: No direct company-specific mapping; use handbook guidance and add your own evidence.
Meaning: Operating business value per dollar of revenue. Includes the cash/debt bridge, making comparisons across capital structures more useful than P/S alone.
Interpretation: Use consistent revenue periods. Consider Revenue Growth, Gross Margin, Operating Margin, expected future margins, capital intensity, Free Cash Flow potential, ROIC, competitive advantage and risk.
Cautions: A multiple is not a valuation by itself. A high multiple does not automatically mean expensive; a low multiple does not automatically mean cheap.
Related cards: enterprise-value, price-sales, gross-margin, operating-margin, capex-efficiency, fcf, roic, moat, embedded-expectations
Additional guidance: A multiple is not a valuation by itself.

AVGO coverage: No direct company-specific mapping; use handbook guidance and add your own evidence.
Meaning: Revenue Growth measures expansion in sales; Profitable Growth asks whether that expansion creates economic value.
Interpretation: Ask: Is Revenue growing? Is Gross Margin stable or improving? Is Operating Margin improving? Is Free Cash Flow improving? Is ROIC improving?
Cautions: Growth alone does not create shareholder value if it permanently destroys capital. Improving ROIC is not sufficient if returns remain below the cost of capital.
Related cards: revenue, gross-margin, operating-margin, fcf, roic, wacc, capex, invested-capital, incremental-roic, capital-allocation, dcf-intro
Additional guidance: Growth does not automatically create shareholder value.  Growth + ROIC > WACC → Potential value creation.  Growth + ROIC < WACC → Potential value destruction.  For new growth, test incremental ROIC: rapid Revenue Growth can destroy value when new investment earns less than its Cost of Capital.

AVGO coverage: No direct company-specific mapping; use handbook guidance and add your own evidence.
Meaning: The direction and durability of operating profitability across periods, not just today’s margin.
Interpretation: Compare quarter-over-quarter, year-over-year and multi-year trends. This reveals whether an early-stage or high-growth company is approaching a sustainable profit model.
Cautions: Control for seasonality, acquisitions, one-off costs and accounting changes. An improving loss is progress, not proof of future profitability.
Additional guidance: Operating Loss  Smaller Operating Loss  Operating Breakeven  Positive Operating Margin  Operating Margin Expansion

AVGO coverage: No direct company-specific mapping; use handbook guidance and add your own evidence.
Meaning: Contracted future business that has not yet been recognized as Revenue. Reported definitions vary by company.
Interpretation: Examine backlog growth, expected recognition period, cancellation risk, customer concentration, contract profitability and conversion into Revenue.
Cautions: Backlog ≠ Revenue. Backlog ≠ Profit. Backlog ≠ Cash Flow. Options, funding conditions and cancellations can change reported totals.

AVGO coverage: No direct company-specific mapping; use handbook guidance and add your own evidence.
Meaning: The likelihood that contracted business converts into profitable revenue and collectible cash.
Interpretation: A large backlog is valuable only if the company can fulfill it profitably. Favor credible customers, realistic delivery schedules and sustainable contract margins.
Cautions: Size alone hides cancellation rights, concentration, fixed-price cost overruns and execution constraints.

AVGO coverage: No direct company-specific mapping; use handbook guidance and add your own evidence.
Meaning: A contract liability generally arising when payment is received, or becomes due, before the related goods or services are transferred.
Interpretation: Customer prepayments can finance operations. Unlike Backlog, Deferred Revenue reflects advance consideration received or due for unfulfilled performance; definitions and overlap must be checked in the notes.
Cautions: Billing is not necessarily cash collection. Do not add Deferred Revenue to Backlog if it is already included in the reported Backlog.
Additional guidance: Illustrative prepaid service:   Customer pays  Cash received  Deferred Revenue liability  Product/service delivered  Revenue recognized

AVGO coverage: No direct company-specific mapping; use handbook guidance and add your own evidence.
Meaning: Sales value announced under signed agreements, often covering several future periods. It is not a standardized substitute for recognized revenue.
Interpretation: Read contract duration, enforceability, cancellation clauses, delivery obligations and collection terms. Distinguish each stage in the comparison below.
Cautions: A press release announcing billions in signed contracts does not mean billions in Revenue were generated during that period. Do not sum overlapping contract metrics.
Additional guidance: Contracted Sales  Signed agreement value; may span years.    Backlog  Contracted business not yet recognized as Revenue. Meaning: Revenue is recorded as promised goods or services are transferred to the customer—at a point in time or over time as performance obligations are satisfied.
Interpretation: An order signals demand; a contract sets obligations; cash collection records payment. Recognition follows delivery/performance under the accounting rules, not simply the signature or payment date.
Cautions: Orders can be cancelled and cash can arrive before or after Revenue. Use accounting policies and contract notes to understand timing.

Meaning: How effectively capital spending produces future economic returns. Falling CapEx is not automatically good; rising CapEx is not automatically bad.
Interpretation: What economic return is the company generating from incremental capital investment? Connect spending to capacity, Revenue, Operating Leverage, Free Cash Flow and ROIC.
Cautions: Compare investment cohorts over appropriate lags. The examples are signals to investigate, not causal proof. Falling spending can reflect underinvestment; high growth can require substantial reinvestment.
